title: Content and distribution
_comment_provides: No role. A role is kernel-initiated work with `cardinality: one` across the whole install, and content is founder-initiated: nothing here should start on a timer before a human has seen what it writes.

find_angles.description: Find where this business's market is ALREADY talking, and what it is asking. Search real threads; return the questions in the words people used, each with the link you found it at. Never invent a forum, a subreddit or a thread — an angle without a URL is a guess dressed as research, and a founder who posts into an invented community loses an afternoon and their trust in this.

sells.description: What this business sells, in the founder's words.

where_they_gather.description: Communities the founder already knows about. A starting point, not a limit.

avoid.description: Places they do not want to appear, and topics they will not touch.

client_summary.description: What their market is actually asking about, in three or four sentences. If you found little, say that — a thin market is a finding and pretending otherwise wastes their month.

question.description: The question people are actually asking, in THEIR words — copied from the thread, not paraphrased into marketing language. "why is my sourdough gummy" is an angle; "optimising bakery operations" is not.

evidence_url.description: The thread, post or page where you saw it. REQUIRED, and it is the whole difference between an angle and a guess: an invented subreddit that sounds plausible is worse than no angle, because a founder posts into it and gets nothing.

where.description: Where the conversation is happening — a subreddit, a forum, a LinkedIn hashtag, a comment section.

asked_by.description: Who is asking: an owner, a customer, a supplier. It decides whether this is a lead or an audience.

why_it_matters.description: What answering it would prove about this business. An angle that does not connect to what they sell is a content idea, not a marketing one.

heat.description: How often you saw it. Honest counts only — 'asked constantly' from one thread is the claim that ends trust in this whole tool.

searched.description: Where you looked, including the places that turned up nothing. A founder cannot tell a thorough search from a lucky one without it.

find_angles._comment_client_facing: Research for the writer. The angles are ours, the post is theirs.
find_angles._comment_ship_requires_client: Research for the writer: the angles are ours, the post is theirs. Its own reason for client_facing: false says so, and a client_summary contradicted it.

plan_content.description: Turn angles and what this business has actually WON into a short plan: what to publish, where, and in what order. Grounded in their own evidence — a plan that could have been written for any business in this trade is a plan nobody follows.

angles.description: From `find_angles`. Each one carries the thread it came from.

wins.description: From the `win-patterns` workflow: which segments actually convert, with sample sizes. The strongest content is about the thing you demonstrably do well, and this is the only honest source for what that is.

weeks.description: How far ahead to plan. Short is better — a twelve-week calendar written before a single post has landed is fiction.

start.description: YYYY-MM-DD, the first day to schedule from. Passed in so the plan is replayable — never read from a clock.

per_week.description: How many pieces a week this founder can genuinely keep to. Default 2. A calendar that assumes five is abandoned in week two, and an abandoned calendar is worse than none because it also carries the evidence that they abandoned it.

what.description: The piece, in one line. Specific enough to write from.

why.description: What it is for: which angle it answers, or which win it proves.

answers_url.description: The thread it replies to, when there is one.

schedule.description: What `content_calendar` returned, quoted verbatim. Never write dates yourself and never re-sort this — a founder who reads Monday's list again on Wednesday has to see the same thing.

cannot_plan.description: True when there is not enough about this business — no audience, no offer, no angles — to plan content that is theirs rather than generic. Then leave `plan` absent.

ship_checks._why: A content plan written without knowing the audience is the most convincing slop this product can produce: it reads like a plan, it is on-topic, and every item would fit any business in the trade.
A content plan whose every item has the same rationale is one idea with four dates on it.

plan_content._comment_calendar: THE MODEL PICKS WHAT AND WHERE; THE WORKFLOW PICKS WHEN. Asking the same run to assign dates is asking a language model to do calendar arithmetic — the same plan run twice would produce two different calendars, 'next Tuesday' would be wrong half the time, and nothing could be checked. `content_calendar` takes the ordered plan and a start date and returns it dated: weekdays only, never twice to one channel in a day, spaced to the cadence the founder can actually keep, and big pieces given the room they need. It PUBLISHES NOTHING and has no network access at all — posting under a founder's own name is public and permanent, and what they need is not a robot with their password, it is to stop opening a blank box on a Sunday night.

sections.heading: What we are publishing, and why now
sections.must: The through-line of the plan tied to what this business has actually won. A paragraph that could have been written for any business in this trade is the failure this task type names in its own description.

sections.heading: The plan
sections.must: Each piece with its channel and its order. Sequence is the deliverable — a list with no order is a brainstorm.

sections.heading: The evidence behind it
sections.must: The angles and wins each piece is grounded in, with the link or the record they came from.

sections.heading: What we need from you
sections.must: Anything the plan cannot start without. If nothing, say so plainly so the client knows they are not blocking it.

write_post.description: Write ONE piece, ready to publish. Grounded in something this business actually did — never a generic post about the trade. It goes to the founder for approval; nothing is ever published from here.

what.description: The piece to write, from the plan.

channel.description: LinkedIn, Reddit, their own blog. It changes the writing, not just the length.

answers_url.description: The thread this replies to, when there is one. Read it before writing — a reply that does not engage with what was actually said is the thing communities ban people for.

facts.description: True things about this business you may use: a result, a number, a thing they built. The post is built from these, and a post with none of them is a post about the industry rather than about them.

client_summary.description: The covering note the founder reads before deciding to post: what this says, who it is for, and what you expect it to do. Not a summary of the post — they can read the post.

channel.description: Where this is meant to go. The same words do not work on LinkedIn and Reddit and it is not a formatting difference — see what-good-content-looks-like.md.

body.description: The post itself, ready to publish. No placeholders, no "[insert stat]", no invented numbers. If a claim needs a figure this business has not given you, write the sentence without it or leave the claim out.

angle_url.description: The thread this answers, when it came from one. It is what makes the post a reply to a real conversation rather than a broadcast.

grounded_in.description: Facts from THIS business that the post relies on — a win, a number, a thing they actually did. Empty means the post is generic, and generic is the failure mode of every content tool ever built.

recommendation.description: What you would do, so the founder answers in one word.

questions.description: What you could not decide alone — a claim you cannot verify, a customer name you may not have permission to use.

needs.description: What only the founder has, and without which this post cannot be written honestly.

artifacts.description: The post as a file in ./output/, plus anything that goes with it.

cannot_write.description: True when the angle has no source to write from, or the business facts needed are absent. Then leave `body` absent.

ship_checks._why: A post written from nothing is indistinguishable from a post written from research until the client's own audience reads it and recognises neither the voice nor the claim.

sections.heading: The post
sections.must: The finished text, ready to publish as written. Not an outline, not a draft with placeholders, not notes toward a post.

sections.heading: Where it goes
sections.must: The channel this was written for, and anything about the format there it has been shaped to.

sections.heading: What it is built on
sections.must: The claims in the post that come from this business's own evidence, and where each came from. Any claim not traceable here should not be in the post.

intake_asks.ask: What have you actually done that you would be happy to talk about publicly?
intake_asks.detail: A result, a project, a number. Content grounded in a real thing is the only kind that works, and this is the only place we can get one.

intake_asks.ask: Anywhere you do NOT want to appear, or anything you will not say?

_comment_intake: A content desk that asks nothing at intake cannot know the audience, and a post written for 'a business audience' is written for nobody. `deliverable-grade` called this out as `needs-nothing`: the service asks for nothing and then produces work that could be about any firm in the trade.

intake.ask: Who is your client's content for, and what do they already believe?
intake.why: This is the one input that decides whether a post lands. Without it every piece is written for 'a business audience', which is nobody.
intake.example: Operations leads at UK logistics firms, 50-500 staff. They already know they need better tracking and have been burned by a failed TMS rollout. Sceptical of anything that sounds like a platform.

intake.ask: Where does that audience actually read, and in what form?
intake.why: A LinkedIn post, a trade newsletter and a long guide are three different jobs. Getting this wrong wastes the whole piece however good the writing is.
intake.example: LinkedIn for the operations leads, and the Logistics Manager newsletter for the buyers above them. Nobody reads our blog directly; it exists to be linked to.

intake.ask: What does your client sound like, and what can they claim?
intake.why: So a post reads as theirs and never asserts a result they cannot stand behind. A claim the client has to walk back costs more than a piece that never ran.
intake.example: Plain, slightly dry, no exclamation marks. They can cite the Halston migration (38% fewer failed deliveries, published with permission) and nothing else by name.
